sections.overview: The northern fulmar looks like a stocky gull but belongs to the tubenoses, the group that includes albatrosses. It spends most of its life at sea and is famous for spitting foul-smelling stomach oil at intruders.
sections.identification: A seabird 45–50 cm long with a wingspan of 102–112 cm. British adults weigh about 770 g and have a wing about 330 mm long. The typical bird is light grey above and white below, with a thick yellow bill whose nostrils form a tube on top. Dark and intermediate colour forms also occur, mainly in Arctic populations.
sections.habitat: It feeds over continental-shelf waters from the Arctic to temperate seas, rarely more than 100 km from shore. It breeds on sea cliffs, in Britain around the coasts of Scotland, Wales, Ireland and parts of England where suitable cliffs exist.
sections.diet: It eats fish, squid and large zooplankton such as amphipods, mostly caught at the surface. It is also an opportunistic scavenger of discarded fish and carrion, and often follows fishing boats.
sections.behavior: It flies low over the water with stiff wingbeats and long glides. At the nest it defends itself and its site by spitting oil. Young birds spend their first four or five years at sea before visiting colonies.
sections.reproduction: A pair lays a single egg, incubated for 52–53 days with both sexes taking turns. The chick fledges after about 46–51 days. Fulmars first breed at around nine years of age, and many pairs reuse the same nest site year after year.
sections.ecology: Fulmars nest in colonies, often mixed with other seabirds such as kittiwakes. On land, foxes and introduced rats can prey on them. They benefit from fishery discards, which may have helped the North Atlantic population to expand over the past two centuries.
sections.conservation: The IUCN Red List classes the species as Least Concern. The UK breeding population was about 350,000 pairs in 2015; it rose 77% between the 1969–70 and 1985–88 censuses, then fell slightly after the early 2000s, and it is Amber-listed. Fulmars are very long-lived: the oldest ringed bird exceeded 41 years.
